glosses: To promote or advantage.
To help the progress of (something); to further.

examples.text: Some see it as in effect the end of the Syrian uprising that began with peaceful protests against Assad’s police state in 2011, with opposition fighters working to advance Turkey’s interests at the expense of the revolution’s goals.

glosses: To promote or advantage.
To raise (someone) in rank or office; to prefer, to promote.

examples.text: After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him.
This, however, was in time evaded by the monarchs, who advanced certain of their own retainers to a level with the ancient peers of the land[…]

glosses: To move forward in space or time.
To move or push (something) forwards, especially forcefully.

examples.text: Whence and what art thou, execrable shape, / That dar'st, though grim and terrible, advance / Thy miscreated front athwart my way / To yonder gates?

glosses: To move forward in space or time.
To make (something) happen at an earlier time or date; to bring forward, to hasten.

examples.text: [S]in and sorrow it were, considering the hardships of this noble and gallant knight, no whit mentioning or weighing those we ourselves have endured, if we were now either to advance or retard the hour of refection beyond the time when the viands are fit to be set before us.

glosses: To move forward in space or time.
To move forwards; to approach.

examples.text: I advanced towards him step by step, stopping sometimes for fear of waking him.
This army recaptured Wu-chʻang, on the right bank of the Yangtze, in 1854, reached Chen-chiang four years later, advanced to Chiu-chiang and threatened Nanking.

glosses: To move forward in space or time.
To provide (money or other value) before it is due, or in expectation of some work; to lend.

examples.text: “I had intended to ask you to advance me a hundred pounds,” said Phineas.

glosses: To move forward in space or time.
To put forward (an idea, argument etc.); to propose.

examples.text: Some ne'er advance a Judgement of their own, / But catch the spreading notion of the Town […].

glosses: To move forward in space or time.
To make progress; to do well, to succeed.

examples.text: Earlier the caller said men were more likely to be in senior positions. Clegg says that's partly because the current maternity leave arrangements make it difficult for women to advance in the workplace.

glosses: To move forward in space or time.
To move forward in time; to progress towards completion.

examples.text: I can promise you that you will feel even less humorous as the evening advances.

glosses: To raise, be raised.
To raise; to lift or elevate.

examples.text: The fringed Curtaines of thine eyes aduance.

glosses: To raise, be raised.
To raise or increase (a price, rate).

examples.text: In February last […] bakers advanced the price of bread sold over the counter in London from 8d. to 8½d. per quartern loaf.

glosses: To raise, be raised.
To increase (a number or amount).
To raise, be raised.

examples.text: an advance in health or knowledge
an advance in rank or office

glosses: An amount of money or credit, especially given as a loan, or paid before it is due; an advancement.

examples.text: Could he ask the cashier privately for an advance? No, the cashier was no good, no damn good: he wouldn't give an advance.
I shall, with pleasure, make the necessary advances.

glosses: An addition to the price; rise in price or value.

examples.text: an advance on the prime cost of goods

glosses: An opening approach or overture, now especially of an unwelcome or sexual nature.

examples.text: For, if it were of any use to recall matters of fact, what is more notorious, than that prince's applying himself first to the church of England? and upon their refusal to fall in with his measures, making the like advances to the dissenters of all kinds, who readily and almost universally complied with him
As the sun fell, so did our spirits. I had tried to make advances to the girl again; but she would have none of me, and so I was not only thirsty but otherwise sad and downhearted.
I felt vaguely he was a sneak, and remained quite unmollified by advances on his side, which, in a boy's barbarous fashion, unless it suited me to be magnanimous, I haughtily ignored.

glosses: Completed before necessary or a milestone event.

examples.text: He made an advance payment on the prior shipment to show good faith.

glosses: Preceding.

glosses: Forward.

examples.text: The scouts found a site for an advance base.

glosses: Causing offense; arousing a visceral reaction of disgust, anger, hatred, sadness, or indignation.

examples.text: Some people find pornography offensive.
An offensive smell.
A survey at Yale University had 63% of students wanting professors to issue “trigger warnings” before saying anything that some might find offensive or could cause painful emotions.

Britain’s police are especially zealous. Officers spend thousands of hours sifting through potentially offensive posts and arrest 30 people a day. Among those collared were a man who ranted about immigration on Facebook and a couple who criticised their daughter’s primary school.

glosses: Relating to an offense or attack, as opposed to defensive.

examples.text: The army's offensive capabilities. An offensive weapon.

In his submission to the UN, [Christof] Heyns points to the experience of drones. Unmanned aerial vehicles were intended initially only for surveillance, and their use for offensive purposes was prohibited, yet once strategists realised their perceived advantages as a means of carrying out targeted killings, all objections were swept out of the way.

glosses: Having to do with play directed at scoring.

examples.text: The offensive coordinator is responsible for ordering all rushing plays.

glosses: An attack.

examples.text: The Marines today launched a major offensive.

In Central Hupeh, the Japanese launched another offensive from the Kingshan region, but instead of moving southwestward to cooperate with another column of theirs to capture Shasi, this column swerved to the northwest and succeeded in capturing Chunghsiang on the Han River.

glosses: The posture of attacking or being able to attack.

examples.text: He took the offensive in the press, accusing his opponent of corruption.

glosses: An attempt to cause damage, injury to, or death of an opponent or enemy.

examples.text: From 1906 to 1960, there were forty-six recorded shark attacks, half of which were fatal.

One particularly damaging, but often ignored, effect of conflict on education is the proliferation of attacks on schools[…]as children, teachers or school buildings become the targets of attacks. Parents fear sending their children to school. Girls are particularly vulnerable to sexual violence.

glosses: An attempt to cause damage, injury to, or death of an opponent or enemy.
Any of several specific maneuvers, skills, or special abilities that a character can use to inflict damage against opponents.

examples.text: Combat in Mimesis Online is nice and simple. You click on your target […] and then keep right-clicking your chosen attack from the drop down menu. Every time you right click on the attack, your character will swing, shoot, etc.

Kleavor has several attacks that it's worth roughly memorising: a charge attack, where it runs at you quickly; a jump attack, that causes a pillar of rock to spike out from under the ground; and a spin attack that does damage in a circle around it.

glosses: An attempt to detract from the worth or credibility of, a person, position, idea, object, or thing, by physical, verbal, emotional, or other assault.

examples.text: They claimed the censorship of the article was an attack on free speech.
“I came down like a wolf on the fold, didn’t I ? Why didn’t I telephone ? Strategy, my dear boy, strategy. This is a surprise attack, and I’d no wish that the garrison, forewarned, should escape. …”

glosses: A time in which one attacks; the offence of a battle.

examples.text: The army timed their attack to coincide with the local celebrations.

glosses: The beginning of active operations on anything.

examples.text: Having washed the plates from dinner, I made an attack on the laundry.

glosses: An attempt to exploit a vulnerability in a computer system.

examples.text: birthday attack; denial-of-service attack

glosses: Collectively, the bowlers of a cricket side.
Any contact with the ball other than a serve or block which sends the ball across the plane of the net.
The three attackmen on the field or all the attackmen of a team.
The sudden onset of a disease or condition.

examples.text: I've had an attack of the flu.

glosses: An active episode of a chronic or recurrent disease.
The onset of a musical note, particularly with respect to the strength (and duration) of that onset.

examples.text: Eric Reed was a curious choice as pianist, since his busy Petersonian attack is the antithesis of Lewis's, but he acquitted himself with panache, […]

glosses: The amount of time taken for the volume of an audio signal to go from zero to maximum level (e.g. an audio waveform representing a snare drum hit would feature a very fast attack, whereas that of a wave washing to shore would feature a slow attack).
The initial sensory impact of a wine.
To apply violent force to someone or something.

examples.text: This species of snake will only attack humans if it feels threatened.
Yesterday, December seventh, 1941, a date which will live in infamy, the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.

glosses: To aggressively challenge a person, idea, etc., with words (particularly in newspaper headlines, because it typesets into less space than \"criticize\" or similar).

examples.text: She published an article attacking the recent pay cuts.
It was puzzling to read a column that claimed to be attacking me, yet espoused the main ideas in my article.
In its God-like prime, The Simpsons attacked well-worn satirical fodder from unexpected angles, finding fresh laughs in the hoariest of subjects.

glosses: To begin to affect; to act upon injuriously or destructively; to begin to decompose or waste.

examples.text: On the fourth of March he was attacked by fever.
Hydrofluoric acid […] attacks the glass.

glosses: To deal with something in a direct way; to set to work upon.

examples.text: We’ll have dinner before we attack the biology homework.
I attacked the meal with a hearty appetite.
He filled a basin with water, and, with an old brush and piece of sandsoap, attacked the stove.

glosses: To aim balls at the batsman’s wicket.
To set a field, or bowl in a manner designed to get wickets.
To bat aggressively, so as to score runs quickly.
To move forward in an active attempt to score a point, as opposed to trying not to concede.

examples.text: Six successive defeats had left them rooted to the bottom of the Premier League table but, clearly under instructions to attack from the outset, Bolton started far the brighter.

glosses: To accelerate quickly in an attempt to get ahead of the other riders.
(Of a chemical species) To approach a chemical species or bond in order to form a bond with it.
Designed or kept for the purpose of confrontation.

examples.text: En 1910, le parti pro-germanique secondait les attaques contre la Chambre des Lords, dont la majorité était patriote.

glosses: Certaines paroles lâchées comme sans dessein, pour sonder l’intention de quelqu’un ou pour le piquer par quelque reproche.

examples.text: Il m’a déjà fait une attaque là-dessus.

glosses: Apparition soudaine, des accès subits de certaines maladies.

examples.text: Cependant la santé du roi Louis donne depuis quelques années de sérieuses inquiétudes. […]. En mars 1480, il présente aux Forges, près de Chinon, une première attaque, un premier ictus.

glosses: Accès d’apoplexie.

examples.text: Une petite gêne à peine perceptible dans ses mouvements indiquait à l’œil averti qu’il avait eu une attaque. Celle-ci n’avait fait d’ailleurs qu’aiguiser son génie.

glosses: Début de l'émission d'un son.

examples.text: L’harmonicorde de Debain, sur lequel Lefébure Wely excellait, était un harmonium pourvu de cordes tendues qui pouvaient être, ou non, frappées pour donner plus de netteté à l’attaque.

glosses: Une ou plusieurs consonnes devant le noyau (voyelle) dans une syllabe. Le reste de la syllabe est la rime.
Essentiellement dans les sports collectifs avec un ballon, action d'une équipe qui tente de marquer.

glosses: Le fait de révéler, de creuser les joints de grains d'une pièce métallique par action d'une solution acide afin de pouvoir les voir au microscope.
